claim: Antibiotic use is a primary driver of antibiotic resistance.
source: Antibiotic use is a primary driver of antibiotic resistance, and reducing antibiotic use is a central strategy for combatting resistance (Gould, 1999; Harbarth and Samore, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior scholarly work (Gould, 1999; Harbarth and Samore, 2005).

claim: Reducing antibiotic use is a central strategy for combatting resistance.
source: Antibiotic use is a primary driver of antibiotic resistance, and reducing antibiotic use is a central strategy for combatting resistance (Gould, 1999; Harbarth and Samore, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior scholarly work (Gould, 1999; Harbarth and Samore, 2005).

claim: Multiple studies have identified cross-sectional relationships between antibiotic use and resistance, especially across European countries and US states.
source: Multiple studies have identified cross-sectional relationships between antibiotic use and resistance, especially across European countries and US states (Goossens et al., 2005; García-Rey et al., 2002; Bronzwaer et al., 2002; Bell et al., 2014; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control et al., 2017; van de Sande-Bruinsma et al., 2008; MacFadden et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: 30% of patients in the UK were prescribed at least one antibiotic per year.
source: A study of outpatient prescribing in the UK found that 30% of patients were prescribed at least one antibiotic per year, with the top 9% of patients receiving 53% of all antibiotics (Shallcross et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a UK study (Shallcross et al., 2017).

claim: The top 9% of patients in the UK received 53% of all antibiotics.
source: A study of outpatient prescribing in the UK found that 30% of patients were prescribed at least one antibiotic per year, with the top 9% of patients receiving 53% of all antibiotics (Shallcross et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a UK study (Shallcross et al., 2017).

claim: The proportion of Medicare beneficiaries who take antibiotics varies by US state and drug class.
source: A study of beneficiaries of Medicare, a national health insurance program that covers that vast majority of Americans 65 and older, found that the proportion of beneficiaries who take antibiotics varies by US state and drug class (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a Medicare study (Zhang et al., 2012).

claim: Outpatient antibiotic prescribing accounts for 80–90% of total medical antibiotic use in the UK and Sweden.
source: We considered only outpatient antibiotic prescribing, which accounts for 80–90% of total medical antibiotic use in the UK and Sweden (Public Health Agency of Sweden and National Veterinary Institute, 2015; ESPAUR Writing Committee, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to reports from the UK and Sweden.

claim: Outpatient antibiotic prescribing is presumed to account for a similar fraction (80-90%) of total medical antibiotic use in the US.
source: and is presumed to account for a similar fraction in the US (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a CDC report and inference from UK/Sweden data.

claim: The analysis included 99.8 million outpatient pharmacy antibiotic prescription fills among 62.4 million unique people during 2011–2014 using the MarketScan database.
source: Our analysis included 99.8 million outpatient pharmacy antibiotic prescription fills among 62.4 million unique people, approximately 20% of the US population, during 2011–2014 using the MarketScan database (Truven Health Analytics, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the MarketScan database.

claim: The 62.4 million unique people in the MarketScan analysis represent approximately 20% of the US population.
source: Our analysis included 99.8 million outpatient pharmacy antibiotic prescription fills among 62.4 million unique people, approximately 20% of the US population, during 2011–2014 using the MarketScan database (Truven Health Analytics, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the MarketScan database and comparison to US population.

claim: In 2011, 34% of people in the MarketScan database received an antibiotic.
source: In 2011, 34% of people received an antibiotic, and 10% of people received 57% of all antibiotic prescriptions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the MarketScan database for 2011.

claim: In 2011, 10% of people in the MarketScan database received 57% of all antibiotic prescriptions.
source: In 2011, 34% of people received an antibiotic, and 10% of people received 57% of all antibiotic prescriptions.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the MarketScan database for 2011.

claim: The distribution of antibiotic use varied by population but was similar across data years.
source: This distribution varied by population but was similar across data years (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: For all drug groups, most people had zero prescriptions for that antibiotic in a given year.
source: For all drug groups, most people had zero prescriptions for that antibiotic in a given year, but antibiotics differed in their distributions (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Antibiotics differed in their distributions of prescriptions across people.
source: For all drug groups, most people had zero prescriptions for that antibiotic in a given year, but antibiotics differed in their distributions (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Annual repeat use made up a steady one-quarter to one-third of annual total use across drugs and states, with the exception of tetracyclines.
source: Annual repeat use made up a steady one-quarter to one-third of annual total use across drugs and states, with the exception of tetracyclines, for which high repeat use was associated with young adults (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), probably for acne treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and its supplements.

claim: For tetracyclines, high repeat use was associated with young adults, probably for acne treatment.
source: Annual repeat use made up a steady one-quarter to one-third of annual total use across drugs and states, with the exception of tetracyclines, for which high repeat use was associated with young adults (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), probably for acne treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, with speculation about acne treatment.

claim: The distribution of first and repeat use is distinct from the pattern predicted by the single-parameter Poisson and geometric distributions.
source: This distribution of first and repeat use is distinct from the pattern predicted by the single-parameter Poisson and geometric distributions (Figure 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data to theoretical distributions shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ratio of first use to repeat use for each drug was nearly constant across US Census regions.
source: but the ratio of first use to repeat use for each drug was nearly constant across US Census regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The higher antibiotic use in the Southern states is primarily attributable to a greater proportion of people taking antibiotics, not because those who receive antibiotics receive more of them.
source: Thus, the higher antibiotic use in the Southern states (Zhang et al., 2012; Hicks et al., 2013) is primarily attributable to a greater proportion of people taking antibiotics, not because those who receive antibiotics receive more of them.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the data on first and repeat use, combined with citations about Southern state antibiotic use.

claim: ResistanceOpen included resistance of 38 pathogens to 37 antibiotics in 641 antibiotic susceptibility reports from 230 organizations spread over 44 US states.
source: To measure antibiotic resistance, we used ResistanceOpen, a US nationwide sample of hospital antibiotic susceptibility reports (MacFadden et al., 2016), which included resistance of 38 pathogens to 37 antibiotics in 641 antibiotic susceptibility reports from 230 organizations (hospitals, laboratories, and surveillance units) spread over 44 US states.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the ResistanceOpen database.

claim: Hospital antibiotic susceptibility reports are biased toward community-acquired organisms.
source: Although most organizations contributing antibiotic susceptibility reports were hospitals, hospital antibiotic susceptibility reports are biased toward community-acquired organisms (Wang et al., 2017; Hindler and Stelling, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Community antibiotic use can drive antibiotic resistance measured in hospitals.
source: community antibiotic use can drive antibiotic resistance measured in hospitals (Knight et al., 2018; MacFadden et al., 2018b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Across 72 pathogen-antibiotic combinations, correlation coefficients between total use and resistance ranged from –32% to 64%.
source: Across those 72 combinations, correlation coefficients ranged from –32% to 64% (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1 - Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1 - Table 2.

claim: The strongest correlation (Spearman's ρ = 64%, 95% CI 41% to 80%) was between macrolide use and the proportion of Streptococcus pneumoniae isolates that were macrolide nonsusceptible.
source: The strongest correlation (Spearman's ρ = 64%, 95% CI 41% to 80%) was between macrolide use and the proportion of Streptococcus pneumoniae isolates that were macrolide nonsusceptible (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Correlation coefficients between antibiotic use and resistance were mostly positive (median correlation coefficient 21%, IQR 8% to 34%).
source: Correlation coefficients were mostly positive (median correlation coefficient 21%, IQR 8% to 34%).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation data.

claim: Use-resistance correlations involving macrolides, quinolones, and cephalosporins were more positive than those for nitrofurantoin.
source: Use-resistance correlations involving macrolides, quinolones, and cephalosporins were more positive than those for nitrofurantoin, and correlations involving quinolones were more positive than those for trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (pairwise Mann-Whitney tests, two-tailed, FDR = 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Mann-Whitney tests) of the correlation data.

claim: Correlations involving quinolones were more positive than those for trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.
source: Use-resistance correlations involving macrolides, quinolones, and cephalosporins were more positive than those for nitrofurantoin, and correlations involving quinolones were more positive than those for trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (pairwise Mann-Whitney tests, two-tailed, FDR = 0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Mann-Whitney tests) of the correlation data.

claim: Coefficients were not significantly more positive for any particular pathogen.
source: Coefficients were not significantly more positive for any particular pathogen.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the correlation data.

claim: Isolates from older adults are disproportionately represented in antibiotic susceptibility reports.
source: Because isolates from older adults are disproportionately represented in antibiotic susceptibility reports (Kanjilal et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: When antibiotic use among Medicare beneficiaries was substituted for antibiotic use as measured in the MarketScan data, correlation coefficients were similar.
source: When antibiotic use among Medicare beneficiaries was substituted for antibiotic use as measured in the MarketScan data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), correlation coefficients were similar (Supplementary file 1 – Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing MarketScan and Medicare results.

claim: Children are the primary carriers for some pathogens (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae).
source: Conversely, children are the primary carriers for some pathogens (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae (García-Rodríguez and Fresnadillo Martínez, 2002))
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Restricting the antibiotic use data to members at most 15 years old yielded similar correlation coefficients.
source: Restricting the antibiotic use data to members at most 15 years old (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) again yielded similar coefficients (Supplementary file 1 - Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data comparing results for children versus all ages.

claim: The landscape of correlations was mostly robust to the exact population in which antibiotic use was measured.
source: Thus, the landscape of correlations we observed was mostly robust to the exact population in which antibiotic use was measured.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the sensitivity analyses comparing different populations.

claim: The absolute values of the correlation coefficients were slightly closer to zero when using days supply rather than fills (Wilcoxon test, two-tailed; pseudomedian difference in absolute correlation coefficient 1.9 percentage points, 95% CI 0.72 to 3.1).
source: The absolute values of the correlation coefficients were slightly closer to zero when using days supply rather than fills (Wilcoxon test, two-tailed; pseudomedian difference in absolute correlation coefficient 1.9 percentage points, 95% CI 0.72 to 3.1)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Wilcoxon test) comparing different metrics of antibiotic use.

claim: The absolute values of the correlation coefficients were substantially closer to zero when using hospital referral regions rather than states as the units of analysis (6.1 percentage points, 95% CI 3.0 to 9.1).
source: and substantially closer to zero when using hospital referral regions rather than states as the units of analysis (6.1 percentage points, 95% CI 3.0 to 9.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing comparing different geographic units of analysis.

claim: Correlations using the resistance data excluding inpatient-only isolates were slightly stronger than the baseline data (Wilcoxon test, two-tailed; pseudomedian difference in absolute correlation coefficient 1.1 percentage points, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.2).
source: Correlations using the resistance data excluding inpatient-only isolates were slightly stronger than the baseline data (Wilcoxon test, two-tailed; pseudomedian difference in absolute correlation coefficient 1.1 percentage points, 95% CI 0.01 to 2.2)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Wilcoxon test) comparing different subsets of resistance data.

claim: Correlations computed using the outpatient-only resistance data were not systematically stronger or weaker than baseline.
source: but correlations computed using the outpatient-only data were not systematically stronger or weaker.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing outpatient-only resistance data to baseline.

claim: Regression coefficients for first use were more often positive than negative (54 of 72 [75%]; binomial test, 95% CI 63% to 84%).
source: Regression coefficients for first use were more often positive than negative (54 of 72 [75%]; binomial test, 95% CI 63% to 84%).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (binomial test) of regression coefficients.

claim: First use was positively associated with resistance when controlling for repeat use.
source: That is, first use was positively associated with resistance when controlling for repeat use.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the multiple regression analysis.

claim: Regression coefficients for repeat use were more often negative than positive (44 of 72 [61%]; binomial test, 95% CI 49% to 72%).
source: In contrast, regression coefficients for repeat use were more often negative than positive (44 of 72 [61%]; binomial test, 95% CI 49% to 72%).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (binomial test) of regression coefficients.

claim: Repeat use was negatively associated with resistance when controlling for first use.
source: That is, repeat use was negatively associated with resistance when controlling for first use.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the multiple regression analysis.

claim: In all sensitivity analyses, regression coefficients for first use in the multiple regression were more likely to be positive than negative.
source: In all cases, regression coefficients for first use in the multiple regression were more likely to be positive than negative, and regression coefficients for repeat use were more likely to be negative than positive in all but one case (Supplementary file 1 - Table 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from sensitivity analyses shown in Supplementary file 1 - Table 5.

claim: Regression coefficients for repeat use were more likely to be negative than positive in all but one sensitivity analysis.
source: In all cases, regression coefficients for first use in the multiple regression were more likely to be positive than negative, and regression coefficients for repeat use were more likely to be negative than positive in all but one case (Supplementary file 1 - Table 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from sensitivity analyses shown in Supplementary file 1 - Table 5.

claim: The study used US nationwide datasets measuring antibiotic use in 60 million individuals and antibiotic resistance in 3 million bacterial isolates.
source: We used US nationwide datasets measuring antibiotic use in 60 million individuals and antibiotic resistance in 3 million bacterial isolates to analyze relationships between antibiotic use and resistance, examining 72 pathogen-antibiotic combinations simultaneously, using identical data sources and analytical methods across combinations.
evidence: The claim is supported by description of the data sources used in the study.

claim: The study examined 72 pathogen-antibiotic combinations simultaneously, using identical data sources and analytical methods across combinations.
source: We used US nationwide datasets measuring antibiotic use in 60 million individuals and antibiotic resistance in 3 million bacterial isolates to analyze relationships between antibiotic use and resistance, examining 72 pathogen-antibiotic combinations simultaneously, using identical data sources and analytical methods across combinations.
evidence: The claim is supported by description of the study methodology.

claim: Previous studies examining multiple pathogen-antibiotic combinations usually consider no more than five pathogens or antibiotics at once.
source: Although previous studies have examined multiple pathogen-antibiotic combinations, usually no more than five pathogens or antibiotics are considered at once (Goossens et al., 2005; García-Rey et al., 2002; van de Sande-Bruinsma et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies and comparison to the current study.

claim: Correlations between total use and resistance were mostly positive.
source: We found that correlations between total use and resistance were mostly positive and that certain drugs tended to have more positive correlations, but that there was no clear pattern by organism (Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of correlations.

claim: Certain drugs tended to have more positive correlations between use and resistance.
source: We found that correlations between total use and resistance were mostly positive and that certain drugs tended to have more positive correlations, but that there was no clear pattern by organism (Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of correlations.

claim: There was no clear pattern by organism in the use-resistance correlations.
source: We found that correlations between total use and resistance were mostly positive and that certain drugs tended to have more positive correlations, but that there was no clear pattern by organism (Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of correlations.

claim: The overall landscape of correlations was mostly robust to the age groups studied, the subset of resistance data used, and the geographic scale of the analysis.
source: The overall landscape of correlations was mostly robust to the age groups studied, the subset of resistance data used, and the geographic scale of the analysis, although correlations were somewhat weaker when conducting analysis at smaller geographic scales (van de Sande-Bruinsma et al., 2008; Priest et al., 2001; Magee et al., 1999; Livermore et al., 2000).

claim: Correlations were somewhat weaker when conducting analysis at smaller geographic scales.

evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and citations to prior studies.

claim: 80–90% of antibiotic use occurs in the outpatient setting.
source: We used outpatient antibiotic use as the predictor of resistance because 80–90% of antibiotic use occurs in the outpatient setting (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a CDC report.

claim: Most antibiotic pressure on pathogens is due to 'bystander selection', in which the patient is treated for some reason other than an infection caused by that pathogen.
source: and because most antibiotic pressure on pathogens is due to 'bystander selection', in which the patient is treated for some reason other than an infection caused by that pathogen (Tedijanto et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

source: For example, for S. pneumoniae and macrolides, Goossens et al. (2005) reported a Spearman's ρ of 83%
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The narrow variation in β-lactam use across US states (approximately two-fold between the highest- and lowest-using states) may obscure a correlation that is more apparent in Europe.
source: We propose that the narrow variation in β-lactam use across US states, approximately two-fold between the highest- and lowest-using states, obscures a correlation that is more apparent in Europe, where there is a four-fold variation between the highest- and lowest-using countries (Goossens et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculation based on comparison of US and European data ranges.

claim: In Europe, there is a four-fold variation in β-lactam use between the highest- and lowest-using countries.
source: We propose that the narrow variation in β-lactam use across US states, approximately two-fold between the highest- and lowest-using states, obscures a correlation that is more apparent in Europe, where there is a four-fold variation between the highest- and lowest-using countries (Goossens et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a European study.

claim: If outpatient antibiotic use selects for resistance among community-acquired infections, and hospital antibiograms reflect data from community-acquired infections as well as unrelated inpatient resistance patterns, then the correlations measured would be biased toward weaker associations.
source: For example, if outpatient antibiotic use selects for resistance among community-acquired infections, and hospital antibiograms reflect data from community-acquired infections as well as unrelated inpatient resistance patterns, then the correlations we measure would be biased toward weaker associations.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential bias in the study design.

claim: Antibiotic use and resistance in the community setting is not completely independent of use and resistance in the hospital setting.
source: Furthermore, antibiotic use and resistance in the community setting is not completely independent of use and resistance in the hospital setting (Knight et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: The cross-sectional approach assumes that antibiotic use is autocorrelated across years or that resistance changes slowly.
source: Second, antibiotic resistance is temporally dynamic, and our cross-sectional approach assumes that antibiotic use is autocorrelated across years (Lipsitch, 2001) or that resistance changes slowly (Hennessy et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies and inference about the study design.

claim: If use causes resistance, and use and resistance changed meaningfully over the course of the study, then the correlations measured by aggregating over all years would be biased toward weaker associations.
source: If use does cause resistance, and use and resistance changed meaningfully over the course of the study, then the correlations we measured by aggregating over all years would be biased toward weaker associations.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential bias in the study design.

claim: Use of one antibiotic can select for resistance to another antibiotic.
source: Third, because of the limitations in statistical power, we did not address the possibility that use of one antibiotic can select for resistance to another antibiotic (Pouwels et al., 2018; Weber et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Use of one antibiotic can select for resistance to another antibiotic if the dominant clones of that species are resistant to both.
source: Notably, use of one antibiotic can select for resistance to another antibiotic if the dominant clones of that species are resistant to both (Pouwels et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: If the use rates of two drugs are correlated across states, and use of one drug selects for resistance to another, then the apparent relationship between one drug and resistance to that drug would be biased upward.
source: In that case, if the use rates of the two drugs are correlated across states, then the apparent relationship between one drug and resistance to that drug would be biased upward.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential bias in the study design.

claim: The palette of antibiotic use varies by country.
source: Furthermore, because the palette of antibiotic use varies by country (Van Boeckel et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Different pathogen strains circulate in different populations.
source: and different pathogen strains circulate in different populations
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The univariate associations observed between use of an antibiotic and resistance to that antibiotic in the US may not be applicable in other geographies.
source: the univariate associations we observed between use of an antibiotic and resistance to that antibiotic in the US may not be applicable in other geographies.
evidence: The claim is inference about the generalizability of the study results.

claim: The measured correlation would be biased if poor patient adherence increased resistance and patient adherence were also correlated with antibiotic use.
source: The measured correlation would then be biased if, for example, poor patient adherence increased resistance and patient adherence were also correlated with antibiotic use.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential bias in the study design.

claim: 34% of the study population took an antibiotic in a year.
source: We described the distribution of antibiotic use across drug groups and US states, finding that 34% of the study population took an antibiotic in a year, and 10% of the population had 57% of the antibiotic fills in that year, similar to results from the UK (Shallcross et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and comparison to UK results.

claim: 10% of the population had 57% of the antibiotic fills in a year.
source: We described the distribution of antibiotic use across drug groups and US states, finding that 34% of the study population took an antibiotic in a year, and 10% of the population had 57% of the antibiotic fills in that year, similar to results from the UK (Shallcross et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study and comparison to UK results.

claim: For each drug, annual first use makes up the majority of annual total use.
source: By partitioning annual total use into annual first use and annual repeat use, we were able to show that, for each drug, annual first use makes up the majority of annual total use and that variations in annual first use explain more variance in annual total use than do variations in annual repeat use.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of first and repeat use.

claim: Variations in annual first use explain more variance in annual total use than do variations in annual repeat use.
source: By partitioning annual total use into annual first use and annual repeat use, we were able to show that, for each drug, annual first use makes up the majority of annual total use and that variations in annual first use explain more variance in annual total use than do variations in annual repeat use.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of first and repeat use.

claim: First use tends to have a positive association with resistance when controlling for repeat use.
source: We also found that first use tends to have a positive association with resistance when controlling for repeat use, while repeat use tends to have negative associations with resistance when controlling for first use.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple regression analysis.

claim: Repeat use tends to have negative associations with resistance when controlling for first use.
source: We also found that first use tends to have a positive association with resistance when controlling for repeat use, while repeat use tends to have negative associations with resistance when controlling for first use.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from multiple regression analysis.

claim: If the associations are causal, antibiotic resistance in the outpatient setting is due more to first use than to repeat use.
source: If these associations are causal, that is, if outpatient first and repeat antibiotic use select for resistance among community-acquired pathogens, then our results would imply that antibiotic resistance in the outpatient setting is due more to first use, which tended to have positive associations with resistance, than to repeat use.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the causal interpretation of the results.

claim: If the associations are causal, preventing marginal prescriptions among patients whose indications are borderline-appropriate or inappropriate for antibiotics may be the more effective tactic for reducing the prevalence of resistance mechanisms already established in the US.
source: In contrast to proposals to focus on intense antibiotic users for combatting resistance (Shallcross et al., 2017), this situation would imply that preventing marginal prescriptions among patients whose indications are borderline-appropriate or inappropriate for antibiotics may be the more effective tactic for reducing the prevalence of resistance mechanisms already established in the US.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the implications of the results for antibiotic stewardship, with a citation to a contrasting proposal.

claim: Factors beyond antibiotic use, like population density, play a role in antibiotic resistance.
source: Factors beyond antibiotic use, like population density, play a role in antibiotic resistance (Harbarth and Samore, 2005; MacFadden et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: If resistance to a drug is high, treatment using that drug is more likely to fail, discouraging repeated use, so that high resistance leads to decreased repeat use.
source: For example, if resistance to a drug is high, treatment using that drug is more likely to fail, discouraging repeated use, so that high resistance lead to decreased repeat use (Wang et al., 2017; Priest et al., 2001; Pouwels et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculation about reverse causation, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ecological studies do not directly address causality.
source: Ecological studies like this one do not directly address causality, and further work is needed to distinguish between different causal pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ecological study designs.

claim: Morbid individuals have more repeat antibiotic use.

evidence: The claim is speculation about the relationship between morbidity and antibiotic use.

claim: Morbid individuals visit the hospital more often, putting them at higher risk of antibiotic resistant infections regardless of their antibiotic use.
source: We also expect that morbid individuals visit the hospital more often, putting them at higher risk of antibiotic resistant infections regardless of their antibiotic use.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the relationship between morbidity and risk of resistant infections.

claim: Failing to control for morbidity biases the association between repeat use and resistance toward more positive values.
source: Thus, we speculate that repeat use causes resistance and also is a predictor of morbidity, which is associated with resistance. Failing to control for morbidity thus biases the association between repeat use and resistance toward more positive values.
evidence: The claim is speculation about potential confounding by morbidity.

claim: Controlling for morbidity would decrease the measured relationships between repeat use and resistance, amplifying the central result.
source: Conversely, controlling for morbidity would decrease the measured relationships between repeat use and resistance, amplifying our central result.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the effect of controlling for morbidity.

claim: The central result held when re-defining first and repeat use with respect to a 4-year period.
source: Although our central result held when re-defining first and repeat use with respect to a 4-year period (Supplementary file 1 - Table 5)
evidence: The claim is supported by data from a sensitivity analysis.

claim: Population-wide antibiotic use and population-wide resistance appears to be more closely linked with broadly distributed, low-intensity use rather than with intensity of use.
source: In conclusion, we find that population-wide antibiotic use and population-wide resistance appears to be more closely linked with broadly distributed, low-intensity use rather than with intensity of use.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the data analysis.

claim: An ideal study would compare the complete history of an individual's outpatient and inpatient antibiotic exposure with clinical microbiology data from that same individual, cross-referenced against population-level factors, among a representative, nationwide sample of individuals.
source: An ideal study would compare the complete history of an individual's outpatient and inpatient antibiotic exposure with clinical microbiology data from that same individual, cross-referenced against population-level factors, among a representative, nationwide sample of individuals.
evidence: The claim is speculation about an ideal study design.

claim: In the absence of an ideal dataset, these ecological, associative results provide a guide to the development of antibiotic stewardship policy.
source: In the absence of such a dataset, these ecological, associative results provide a guide to the development of antibiotic stewardship policy.
evidence: The claim is inference about the utility of the study results.

claim: Only members who were on their insurance plan for 12 months during a given calendar year were included in the MarketScan analysis.
source: To ensure quality of the antibiotic use distribution data, only members who were on their insurance plan for 12 months during a given calendar year were included.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological choice in the study design.

claim: Antibiotic use was measured using fills, rather than days supply of drug, because some previous research has suggested that prescriptions better correlate with resistance.
source: In the main analysis, antibiotic use was measured using fills, rather than days supply of drug, because some previous research has suggested that prescriptions better correlate with resistance (Bruyndonckx et al., 2015) and that this choice is probably not detrimental (van de Sande-Bruinsma et al., 2008; Lipsitch, 2001).
evidence: The claim describes a methodological choice supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ResistanceOpen database contains approximately 86,000 records of antibiotic resistance data from online sources during 2012 to 2015.
